title_original: Tallinn Black Nights Fest Awards: ‘On Top of the Cliff’ Scores Grand Prix, ’When She Hears the Bells’ Bags Best First Feature
excerpt_original: Latin-America and European cinema triumphed at Friday’s awards ceremony of Tallinn’s Black Nights Film Festival whose fame for discoveries was born out one more year by its final winners, including in its industry section. For her first year as Artistic Director, Triin Tramberg…

blocks.text: Latin-America and European cinema triumphed at Friday’s awards ceremony of Tallinn’s Black Nights Film Festival whose fame for discoveries was born out one more year by its final winners, including in its industry section.
For her first year as Artistic Director, Triin Tramberg had prioritized mixing second time directors with established names in the official selection, a bet which looks to have paid off.

blocks.text: The biggest award at Tallinn Black Nights, known as PÖFF, the €20,000 ($22,000) Grand Prix from the City of Tallinn was handed out by a jury chaired by Sir Christopher Hampton , to “On Top of the Cliff,” the sophomore feature from Peruvian-born Enrica Perez (“Climas)”. Its lead, newcomer Bianca Bucelli, also earned a best actress nod.

The co-production between Perú, Mexico and Switzerland is a psycho thriller about faith, obsession and control, set within a secluded Catholic girls’ boarding school on the cliffs of 1950’s Lima. Reason8 handles sales.

“Among a number of extremely accomplished entries, the jury was especially impressed by the high quality of every department of this film – direction, script, acting, cinematography, design and music – combining to create a hermetic universe, intense, powerful and visually eloquent,” said the jury.

Another female second time director – Germany’s Alison Kuhn – was hailed for her script of “The Matriarch.” The first film with an almost exclusively Vietnamese-German cast, was praised for its “immersion in a community rarely represented on screen, and its nuanced and sensitive exploration of a mother-daughter relationship that navigates the blurred boundaries between right and wrong, care and cruelty, and the harsh rules imposed by the need to survive.” Pluto Film is its sales agent.

Making his screen debut in “The Assignment” by seasoned Belgian helmer Patrice Toy, Mathisse De Sutter was singled out in the acting category for “his ability to depict the tenderness and emotional depth he brought to a story about masculinity in the aftermath of war.”

Two buzzy titles were distinguished for their craft achievements: Patricia Ortega’s biopic “Caballé” – a flagship title in the Basque region’s Special Focus in Tallinn, and Ireland’s “One Sweet Hour” by Declan Recks. Within the highly competitive First Feature slot, the top win went to the anti-Taliban female-driven pic “ When She Hears the Bells ,” by Chabname Zariab and headlined by Golshifteh Farahani. “It is a tense, emotional story of resistance and courage that kept us on the edge of our seats. We were hugely impressed to see a debut with such scale and energy and congratulate the filmmakers on a vital story that will stay with us for a long time, said the jury, headed by seasoned producer Ivana MacKinnon (“How to Have Sex”).

Established Danish doc helmer and war reporter Naieb Khaja took Best Director for his debut fiction “Lionheart” set on Copenhagen’s gang scene, while Polish helmer Sonja Orlewicz-Zakrzewska’s “Exotic” picked a split Special Jury Prize. “The tender, human and generous film got under our skin and gave us access to a unique world. We had a great time watching this film!” said the jury about the pic set in the pole dancing community. Pluto Film handles sales.

In the boundary-pushing section Rebels with a Cause, overseen by Javier Garcia Puerto, the top honor went to the U.S. indie “Pop Pop” by Dylan Stephen Levers, produced by the helmer with W. Ian Ross and Consuelo Althouse.

“Made with an undeniable independent spirit, you can feel the sheer determination of its filmmakers to will this work into existence. Urgent, vital, and unafraid to challenge, this is exactly the kind of rebellious filmmaking we need more than ever in these divisive times,” said jurors Jason Wood, Samuel Abrahams, Mireia Vilapuig.

Meanwhile in the Critics’ Picks curated by the well-known Nikolaj Nikitin, the top prize went to Bulgarian helmer Maya Vitkova-Kosev (“Viktoria”) for “One Month, a work which jurors Heike-Melba Fendel, Jurgis Matulevičius and Hakim Zejjari said will “most certainly remain in our minds and in our hearts.”
International docs that made their mark included the Danish pics “The War We Carry” and “Father’s House” which took home respectively Best Film and a Special Award from the Doc Competition.

Baltic Blast In a year where the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were under the limelight, gloriously celebrated at the festival which also turned 30 this year, some of the region’s brightest stars were profusely applauded tonight at Tallinn’s Alexela Concert Hall. Projects pitched at the Industry & Tallinn & Baltic Event also topped the award list.

Lithuania’s newcomer Danielus Minkevicius shared a Jury Special Award from the First Feature competition for “Oblivion,” which played for the jurors as “an intimate, deeply moving work from a bold new voice in Baltic cinema.”

In the Baltic Competition section, three titles which played at earlier festivals impressed Tallinn’s jury: the Sundance winner and Lithuania’s Oscar hopeful “How to Divorce During the War” by Andrius Blaževičius’ won Best Film, Latvia’s top helmer Linda Olte Best Directing for “The Child” while the Cannes Special Screening “Vesna” scored a nod for its Baltic co-producers, Stasys Baltakis and Helena Pokorny.

In the doc section, which included several minority Baltic co-productions, Spanish helmers Pepe Andreu and Rafa Molés won best film for “La Pietà,” co-produced with Iceland and Lithuania, and a special nod went to Latvia’s “Riga My Love” by Karolina Peterson.

In the Co-Production Market, the project “Wild Love” from Lithuanian genre specialist Jonas Trukana bagged the coveted €20,000 ($22,000) Eurimages Co-Production Development Award for “its audacity to go beyond genre conventions, to convey a timely message, and for the ambition to unite a region behind common values such as care, integrity, independence and sense of humour,” said jurors Stefan Prohorov, Holly Daniel and Ivo Felt. The project produced by Klementina Remeikaitė & Rūta Kiaupaitė for Afterschool also won the Apostlab Scholarship.

Slava Ukraine As always since the start of war in Ukraine, the country and its inspiring people were at the core of PÖFF’s closing act. Ukraine Film Agency’s head Andrii Osipov solemnly awarded PÖFF’s founder Tiina Lokk the Ukraine’s Order of Princess Olga, Third Class, in recognition of her support for Ukrainian cinema and its international promotion. He also shared with Lokk the honor to grant Halkawt Mustafa’s “No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman” the first ever Free World Award.

To boost Ukraine, “in the light of the ongoing conflict”, the Council of Europe’s also granted its Eurimages Special Co-production Award worth €20,000 ($22,000) to newcomer Victoria Zadorska for “My 19-Year-Old Granny,” produced by Tatofilm, with Greta Akcijonaite from Lithuania and Matej Paclik from Czechia.

In her closing note, Lokk said she was stepping back, ready to wear ‘only’ the cap of festival director, not artistic director now fitfully worn by Tramberg who already proved her programming skills as 124 public screenings at the festival were sold out. “This is the best feeling ever when you have happy people in a cinema next to you!” said Lokk.
